evidence.reasoning:
Source shows a real format-string sink and an unterminated stack buffer used as a C string.

In dissect_bat_vis_v24:
- vis_packeth_raw_data is a 1024-byte stack array.
- vis_packeth_raw_data_size is read from the packet and only checked to be <= sizeof(vis_packeth_raw_data). There is no NUL termination written after the for-loop copy.
- snprintf(d_output_buffer, ..., "... %s", vis_packeth_raw_data) treats vis_packeth_raw_data as a C string; if the copied bytes contain no NUL, snprintf will read past the end of the 1024-byte stack buffer (OOB read) until it finds a 0 byte, which ASan can report/crash.
- Later, if (vis_packeth_raw_data_size > 4) && (strlen(vis_packeth_raw_data) > 4) then fprintf(stderr, d_output_buffer) is called. This is an attacker-controlled format string (d_output_buffer contains raw_data bytes) and can crash (e.g., %s/%n) by reading/writing invalid addresses.

Thus a fuzzer input can drive a SEGV/ASan crash via either the OOB read in snprintf/strlen or the format-string in fprintf.

I attempted to run reach_probe to ground with an input containing "%s%s%s%s" but the probe infrastructure failed (missing ASan binary path), so no runtime confirmation is available.
evidence.corrected_description: Two issues in dissect_bat_vis_v24: (1) stack-buffer over-read because vis_packeth_raw_data is filled with up to 1024 bytes from the packet without NUL termination, then used as a C string in snprintf() and strlen(); (2) format-string vulnerability because fprintf(stderr, d_output_buffer) uses attacker-influenced data as the format string (d_output_buffer includes raw_data). Either can lead to SEGV/ASan crash.
evidence.control_flow_to_bug: handler_bat.vis -> ... -> dissect_bat_vis_v24(tvb,...): read vis_packeth_raw_data_size from tvb; if size <= 1024 copy size bytes into stack vis_packeth_raw_data without appending '\0'; if tree != NULL call snprintf(d_output_buffer, ..., "%s", vis_packeth_raw_data) (may over-read if no NUL in first 1024 bytes); later if vis_packeth_raw_data_size>4 and strlen(vis_packeth_raw_data)>4 call fprintf(stderr, d_output_buffer) where d_output_buffer contains attacker-controlled '%' sequences from raw_data, potentially causing SEGV.

args.generator_code:
def generate()->bytes:
    # Construct minimal BAT_VIS v24-like packet for dissector.
    # Layout inferred from code: ipv4(4) + ?(4) then at offset 8: version, gw_class, tq_max, raw_data_size(u32?)
    # Code uses tvb_get_uint32(tvb, offset++, 0); then offset +=4, so raw_data_size read starting at 11.
    # We'll just provide enough bytes.
    raw = b"%s%s%s%s"  # format string to trigger fprintf reading stack
    raw_size = len(raw)
    pkt = bytearray()
    pkt += b"\x01\x02\x03\x04"      # sender_ip
    pkt += b"\x00\x00\x00\x00"      # padding/unknown
    pkt += b"\x18"  # version
    pkt += b"\x00"  # gw_class
    pkt += b"\x00"  # tq_max
    # raw_data_size: place 4 bytes; but function reads with offset++ then offset+=4, odd.
    # Put size at next 4 bytes.
    pkt += raw_size.to_bytes(4,'big')
    pkt += raw
    # add some trailing bytes for later fields
    pkt += b"\x00"*32
    return bytes(pkt)

full_messages.content:
You are a vulnerability verifier. All candidate functions are already
reachable from the fuzzer — do NOT re-litigate reachability as pass/fail. Your job
is to gather EVIDENCE about whether the reached code actually contains a
crashing memory-safety bug of the stated type, then submit it.

Gather evidence with the tools:
- read_function(name): read the real source.
- check_reachability(function_name): confirm the call graph (depth, direct/indirect).
- reach_probe(generator_code, target): write Python `def generate()->bytes` that
  produces an input aiming to REACH `target` (a function name or "file.c:LINE").
  It runs the input on the real ASan binary under gdb and tells you whether the
  target was reached and whether it crashed. A crash is proof; a reach grounds
  your judgment. Only a real crash or reach can raise the score above the ceiling —
  you cannot assert a high score from reading alone.
- submit_evidence(...): report your structured findings (see its schema). Call it
  once, last.

Two of the fields are NOT about scoring — they correct the SP for the downstream
PoV stage, and you are the right one to write them because you just read the real
code (and maybe ran a reach_probe):
- corrected_description: if the SP's stated bug type/description is wrong or
  imprecise given the real code, write the accurate one (else restate it).
- control_flow_to_bug: the real path from the fuzzer entry to the crash site — the
  key functions, branches, and conditions that must hold to trigger it.

Do NOT pass things "when in doubt". Report what the evidence shows. Absence of a
crash is not proof of safety; a proven clamp/guard on the tainted value IS
disconfirming.

Verify this suspicious point.

Fuzzer: handler_bat.vis   Sanitizer: address
Function: dissect_bat_vis_v24
Claimed bug type: SEGV
Suspicious-point description (from the finder — may be imprecise): `vis_packeth_raw_data` (a 1024-byte stack buffer) is filled from the packet without forcing NUL-termination, then `snprintf(d_output_buffer, ..., "...%s", vis_packeth_raw_data)` and especially `fprintf(stderr, d_output_buffer)` -- an attacker-controlled format string -- are used; the format-string bug (and strlen on the unterminated buffer) crash.

Control flow to the bug:
  - handler_bat.vis; dissect_bat_vis_v24 reads raw_data_size (<=1024) bytes into a stack buffer
  - d_output_buffer is built from the non-terminated raw_data
  - fprintf(stderr, d_output_buffer) uses attacker data as a format string -> SEGV

The function is reachable (confirm with check_reachability if useful).

Read the function, judge whether a fuzzer input can drive a SEGV
there, optionally reach_probe a candidate input to ground it, then submit_evidence.
